newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Technology, customer needs shake up Australia banks.
newsitem.headline: Technology, customer needs shake up Australia banks.

text.p: New technology, changing customer needs and industry regulation changes are behind the recommend shake-up to Australia's financial system, the inquiry into the financial industry said in its report on Wednesday.

However, the recommended changes by the Wallis report, including the end of the "six pillars policy" is likely to lead to a polarisation of financial players in the industry between large conglomerates and small niche players.
"Technological innovation has been a major force shaping financial service delivery over the past two decades and appears likely to accelerate over the next few years," the report said.
The 770 page Wallis report said about 47 percent of Australian households owned personal computers and 15 percent owned modems and people were increasingly using telephone banking.

"...As the Internet becomes more widely accessible and security is improved through technologies such as encryption and authentication, it becomes more likely that households will conduct their financial transations over the Internet," it said. The report said the increase in technology use would accelerate due to the falling cost of technology and proposed better security of electronic transactions.

"These factors will facilitate the conduct of financial activities through homes, workplaces and other sites physically remote from service providers, further reduce cost and lower entry barriers to new suppliers," the report said.
It said consumers would probably rely increasingly on trusted names, resulting in brands of preferred financial system suppliers or advisors becoming very valuable.

"The emergence of new players will be matched by the continued evolution of large financial conglomerates, using their brand and other strengths to provide a wide range of financial services," the report said.

The report said these trends might eventually lead to a polarisation of Australia's whole financial market. "The market may come to be polarised into large and small players, with relatively fewer participants of middle size," the report said.
It said globalisation of the world's financial markets had mainly affected the financial wholesale markets, the retail market had been scarcely affected, but this should change.
"Global retail electronic financial transactions are likely to emerge in the near future and will almost certainly flourish over the period to 2010," the report said.
The report said technology would make it easier for foreign markets to attract investors away from domestic markets.
"As globalisation increases, investors will increasingly be represented by global funds managers with scant loyalities to products or markets," it said
"They will buy shares, bonds, mortgages and other financial products wherever the price is the most attractive," it said.
The report said the impact of changing customer needs were also behind the need to reform Australia's financial industry.
The report said households are increasing relying on the financial system through higher household financial asset holdings and increased borrowing from the financial sector.
It said there was more customer awareness of products and pursing lower cost products, which was creating a more competitive market place.
The Wallis report also recommended mergers between Australia's major banks and life offices and it lifted the blanket ban on Australian bank takeovers by foreigners.
